claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Betz et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2001; Dulubova et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Both Munc13-1 and Rab3A had significantly weaker binding ability with RIM1α in Rapgef3/4-dKO synaptosomes compared to WT.
claims.source: By measuring the ratios of IP/input in co-IP assay of synaptosome extracts, we found that both Munc13-1 and Rab3A had significantly weaker binding ability with RIM1α in both Rapgef3/4-dKO (Figure 2G) and Prkce-cKO (Figure 2H) synaptosomes, as compared to WT and Prkcef/f respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: Both Munc13-1 and Rab3A had significantly weaker binding ability with RIM1α in Prkce-cKO synaptosomes compared to Prkcef/f.
claims.source: By measuring the ratios of IP/input in co-IP assay of synaptosome extracts, we found that both Munc13-1 and Rab3A had significantly weaker binding ability with RIM1α in both Rapgef3/4-dKO (Figure 2G) and Prkce-cKO (Figure 2H) synaptosomes, as compared to WT and Prkcef/f respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: Neither EPAC nor PKCε ablation changed the expression levels of Rab3A and Munc13.
claims.source: In contrast, neither EPAC nor PKCε ablation changed the expression levels of Rab3A and Munc13 (Figure 2G and H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claims.claim: The deficiency of either EPAC or PKCε impairs protein interactions in the Rab3A-RIM1α-Munc13-1 complex.
claims.source: These data indicate that the deficiency of either EPAC or PKCε impairs protein interactions in the Rab3A-RIM1α-Munc13-1 complex.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from co-IP data showing reduced binding of Munc13-1 and Rab3A to RIM1α in EPAC and PKCε knockout mice.

claims.claim: 8-pCPT treatment of WT synaptosomes significantly increased the amount of Munc13-1 and Rab3A precipitated with RIM1.
claims.source: First, we treated WT synaptosomes with 8-pCPT and εV1-2, and measured the amount of Munc13-1 and Rab3A precipitated with RIM1. The quantification showed a significant increment of precipitated Munc13-1 and Rab3A when synaptosomes were incubated with 8-pCPT (Figure 2I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: FR236924 treatment of WT synaptosomes increased precipitations of Munc13-1 and Rab3A with RIM1.
claims.source: Second, we measured the amounts of precipitated Munc13-1 and Rab3A in WT synaptosomes treated with FR236924, a selective activator of PKCε. We found that precipitations of Munc13-1 and Rab3A were both increased (Figure 2J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 2J.

claims.claim: FR236924 is a selective activator of PKCε.
claims.source: Second, we measured the amounts of precipitated Munc13-1 and Rab3A in WT synaptosomes treated with FR236924, a selective activator of PKCε.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the text.

claims.claim: Either EPAC or PKCε is sufficient to promote the formation of the tripartite complex.
claims.source: These data indicate that either EPAC or PKCε is sufficient to promote the formation of the tripartite complex.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing EPAC or PKCε activation increases binding of Munc13-1 and Rab3A to RIM1.

claims.claim: PKCε inhibitor εV1-2 prevented the increase of precipitated Munc13-1 and Rab3A induced by 8-pCPT.
claims.source: In parallel experiments, PKCε inhibitor εV1-2 prevented the increase of precipitated Munc13-1 and Rab3A induced by 8-pCPT (Figure 2I), while FR236924 failed to induce more precipitations of Munc13-1 and Rab3A in Prkce-cKO synaptosomes (Figure 2K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: FR236924 failed to induce more precipitations of Munc13-1 and Rab3A in Prkce-cKO synaptosomes.
claims.source: In parallel experiments, PKCε inhibitor εV1-2 prevented the increase of precipitated Munc13-1 and Rab3A induced by 8-pCPT (Figure 2I), while FR236924 failed to induce more precipitations of Munc13-1 and Rab3A in Prkce-cKO synaptosomes (Figure 2K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 2K.

claims.claim: The EPAC-PKCε module regulates synaptic organization and transmitter release by regulating the stability of Rab3A-RIM1α-Munc13-1 complex.
claims.source: In summary, these data demonstrate that the EPAC-PKCε module regulates synaptic organization and transmitter release by regulating the stability of Rab3A-RIM1α-Munc13-1 complex.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing EPAC-PKCε module affects binding of Rab3A and Munc13-1 to RIM1α, vesicle docking, and transmitter release.

claims.claim: Repetitive stimuli of PF terminals result in an increased Pr of neurotransmitters, leading to the expression of presynaptic LTP.
claims.source: Repetitive stimuli of PF terminals result in an increased Pr of neurotransmitters, leading to the expression of presynaptic LTP (Salin et al., 1996; Kimura et al., 1998; van Beugen et al., 2013; Hirano et al., 2016; Kaeser et al., 2008; Yang and Calakos, 2010; Martín et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Salin et al., 1996; Kimura et al., 1998; van Beugen et al., 2013; Hirano et al., 2016; Kaeser et al., 2008; Yang and Calakos, 2010; Martín et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Tetanus stimulation (8 Hz for 5 min) induced potentiation of EPSCs to 131 ± 6% of baseline in WT mice.
claims.source: The potentiation of EPSCs reached 131 ± 6% of baseline in WT mice (t=38–40 min; n=13; p<0.001; Figure 3B and C), consistent with previous work (Salin et al., 1996; Kaeser et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3B and C, and is consistent with previous work (Salin et al., 1996; Kaeser et al., 2008).

claims.claim: Tetanus stimulation (8 Hz for 5 min) decreased PPF ratio to 84 ± 4% in WT mice.
claims.source: Concomitantly, paired-pulse facilitation (PPF) ratio decreased to 84 ± 4% (t=38–40 min; n=13; p<0.001; Figure 3C), indicating a presynaptic contribution to this form of LTP (Salin et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3C, and is consistent with previous work (Salin et al., 1996).

claims.claim: Preincubation of WT slices with forskolin prevented tetanus stimulation from inducing synaptic potentiation in PCs.
claims.source: Next, we preincubated WT slices with forskolin for 20 min to ensure the effect of forskolin. In this condition, the tetanus stimulation for presynaptic LTP failed to induce synaptic potentiation in PCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating that presynaptic LTP at PF-PC synapses occurs upon a rise in the cellular level of cAMP.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Presynaptic LTP at PF-PC synapses occurs upon a rise in the cellular level of cAMP.
claims.source: Next, we preincubated WT slices with forskolin for 20 min to ensure the effect of forskolin. In this condition, the tetanus stimulation for presynaptic LTP failed to induce synaptic potentiation in PCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating that presynaptic LTP at PF-PC synapses occurs upon a rise in the cellular level of cAMP.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that preincubation with forskolin (which increases cAMP) prevents further LTP induction.

claims.claim: 8 Hz stimulation failed to induce potentiation of EPSCs in Rapgef3/4-dKO mice.
claims.source: We made whole-cell recordings from PCs and found that 8 Hz stimulation failed to induce potentiation of EPSCs in Rapgef3/4-dKO mice (104 ± 5% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=11; p=0.66) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claims.claim: Presynaptic PF-PC LTP was blocked in Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO mice.
claims.source: This finding was confirmed in recordings from slices of Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO mice, in which EPAC is deleted from the granule cells innervating the PCs, showing that presynaptic PF-PC LTP was also blocked (93 ± 4% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=9; p=0.059) (Figure 3F and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claims.claim: The potentiation of EPSCs reached 120 ± 5% of baseline in Atoh1Cre mice following 8 Hz stimulation.
claims.source: In control experiments using Atoh1Cre mice, the potentiation of EPSCs reached 120 ± 5% of baseline (t=38–40 min; n=10; p=0.004; Figure 3D and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claims.claim: Presynaptic EPAC is required for presynaptic LTP.
claims.source: These results indicate that presynaptic EPAC is required for presynaptic LTP.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing presynaptic LTP is blocked in mice with EPAC deletion in granule cells.

claims.claim: The potentiation of PF-EPSCs evoked by 8 Hz stimulation reached 120 ± 3% of baseline in control Prkcef/f mice.
claims.source: Similar to WT and Atoh1Cre mice, the potentiation of PF-EPSCs evoked by 8 Hz stimulation reached 120 ± 3% of baseline in control Prkcef/f mice (t=38–40 min; n=7; p=0.004; Figure 3H and I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3H and I.

claims.claim: Presynaptic ablation of PKCε completely blocked the induction of presynaptic LTP.
claims.source: However, presynaptic ablation of PKCε completely blocked the induction of this form of LTP (99 ± 5%; n=10; p=0.065; Figure 3J and K), suggesting that presynaptic PF-PC LTP also requires PKCε.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3J and K.

claims.claim: Presynaptic PF-PC LTP requires PKCε.
claims.source: However, presynaptic ablation of PKCε completely blocked the induction of this form of LTP (99 ± 5%; n=10; p=0.065; Figure 3J and K), suggesting that presynaptic PF-PC LTP also requires PKCε.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing presynaptic LTP is blocked in mice with PKCε deletion in granule cells.

claims.claim: εV1-2 completely blocked the induction of presynaptic PF-PC LTP in WT mice.
claims.source: This conclusion was further confirmed following chemical inhibition of PKCε by continuously administering εV1-2 to cerebellar slices from WT mice, as εV1-2 completely blocked the induction of presynaptic PF-PC LTP (101 ± 4%; n=9; p=0.59; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F.

claims.claim: 8 Hz stimulation induced a potentiation of EPSCs to 120 ± 4% of baseline in 2-month-old Atoh1Cre mice.
claims.source: In control experiments with Atoh1Cre mice, 8 Hz stimulation induced a potentiation of EPSCs (120 ± 4% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=7; p=0.002) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: 8 Hz stimulation failed to induce potentiation in 2-month-old Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO mice.
claims.source: In contrast, the same stimulation failed to induce the potentiation in Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO mice (97 ± 1% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.76) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Presynaptic PF-PC LTP was successfully induced in 2-month-old Prkcef/f mice.
claims.source: Similarly, presynaptic PF-PC LTP was successfully induced in 2-month-old Prkcef/f mice (119 ± 1% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p<0.001) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), but not in Prkce-cKO mice of the same age (98 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=7; p=0.34) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: Presynaptic PF-PC LTP was not induced in 2-month-old Prkce-cKO mice.
claims.source: Similarly, presynaptic PF-PC LTP was successfully induced in 2-month-old Prkcef/f mice (119 ± 1% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p<0.001) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), but not in Prkce-cKO mice of the same age (98 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=7; p=0.34) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: Presynaptic LTP was induced in Atoh1Cre mice at elevated temperature (32 °C).
claims.source: We found that presynaptic LTP was induced in Atoh1Cre (124 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.00012) and Prkcef/f mice (122 ± 1% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p<0.001) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and C), but not in Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO (97 ± 3% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.33) and Prkce-cKO (100 ± 1% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.92) mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Presynaptic LTP was induced in Prkcef/f mice at elevated temperature (32 °C).
claims.source: We found that presynaptic LTP was induced in Atoh1Cre (124 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.00012) and Prkcef/f mice (122 ± 1% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p<0.001) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and C), but not in Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO (97 ± 3% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.33) and Prkce-cKO (100 ± 1% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.92) mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: Presynaptic LTP was not induced in Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO mice at elevated temperature (32 °C).
claims.source: We found that presynaptic LTP was induced in Atoh1Cre (124 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.00012) and Prkcef/f mice (122 ± 1% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p<0.001) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and C), but not in Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO (97 ± 3% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.33) and Prkce-cKO (100 ± 1% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.92) mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: Presynaptic LTP was not induced in Prkce-cKO mice at elevated temperature (32 °C).
claims.source: We found that presynaptic LTP was induced in Atoh1Cre (124 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.00012) and Prkcef/f mice (122 ± 1% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p<0.001) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and C), but not in Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO (97 ± 3% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.33) and Prkce-cKO (100 ± 1% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.92) mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D.

claims.claim: Presynaptic LTP was induced in Atoh1Cre mice with lowered Ca2+ concentration (0.5 mM) in aCSF.
claims.source: Again, presynaptic LTP was induced in Atoh1Cre (113 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.002) and Prkcef/f mice (113 ± 5% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.002) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and C), but not in Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO (99 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.61) and Prkce-cKO (104 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.53) mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B and D ).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claims.claim: Presynaptic LTP was induced in Prkcef/f mice with lowered Ca2+ concentration (0.5 mM) in aCSF.
claims.source: Again, presynaptic LTP was induced in Atoh1Cre (113 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.002) and Prkcef/f mice (113 ± 5% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.002) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and C), but not in Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO (99 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.61) and Prkce-cKO (104 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.53) mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B and D ).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

claims.claim: Presynaptic LTP was not induced in Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO mice with lowered Ca2+ concentration (0.5 mM) in aCSF.
claims.source: Again, presynaptic LTP was induced in Atoh1Cre (113 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.002) and Prkcef/f mice (113 ± 5% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.002) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and C), but not in Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO (99 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.61) and Prkce-cKO (104 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.53) mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B and D ).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claims.claim: Presynaptic LTP was not induced in Prkce-cKO mice with lowered Ca2+ concentration (0.5 mM) in aCSF.
claims.source: Again, presynaptic LTP was induced in Atoh1Cre (113 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.002) and Prkcef/f mice (113 ± 5% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.002) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and C), but not in Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO (99 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.61) and Prkce-cKO (104 ± 2% of baseline at t=38–40 min; n=6; p=0.53) mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B and D ).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4D.

claims.claim: The function of EPAC and PKCε in the induction of presynaptic PF-LTP is independent of animal age, recording temperature, or external Ca2+ concentration.
claims.source: These experiments indicate that the function of EPAC and PKCε in the induction of presynaptic PF-LTP is independent of animal age, recording temperature, or external Ca2+ concentration.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing EPAC and PKCε are required for presynaptic LTP under different experimental conditions (age, temperature, Ca2+ concentration).

claims.claim: The presynaptic EPAC-PKCε module is critical for presynaptic PF-PC LTP in the cerebellum.
claims.source: Therefore, on the basis of our experiments in PCs from mice with presynaptic specific deletion of EPAC and PKCε, we conclude that the presynaptic EPAC-PKCε module is critical for presynaptic PF-PC LTP in the cerebellum.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing presynaptic deletion of EPAC or PKCε blocks presynaptic LTP.

claims.claim: cAMP is required for presynaptic LTP induced by electrical stimulation.
claims.source: cAMP is also required for presynaptic LTP induced by electrical stimulation (Salin et al., 1996; Le Guen and De Zeeuw, 2010), and its agonists are enough to produce a prominent increase in glutamate release (Weisskopf et al., 1994; Salin et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Salin et al., 1996 and Le Guen and De Zeeuw, 2010.

claims.claim: cAMP agonists are enough to produce a prominent increase in glutamate release.
claims.source: cAMP is also required for presynaptic LTP induced by electrical stimulation (Salin et al., 1996; Le Guen and De Zeeuw, 2010), and its agonists are enough to produce a prominent increase in glutamate release (Weisskopf et al., 1994; Salin et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Weisskopf et al., 1994 and Salin et al., 1996.

claims.claim: The role of PKA in presynaptic LTP has been contradicted by studies showing that presynaptic LTP is intact when serine phosphorylation of RIM1 by PKA is interrupted.
claims.source: The role of PKA in presynaptic LTP has been contradicted by the studies showing that presynaptic LTP is intact when serine phosphorylation of RIM1 by PKA is interrupted (Kaeser et al., 2008; Yang and Calakos, 2010; also see Lonart et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kaeser et al., 2008; Yang and Calakos, 2010; and Lonart et al., 2003.

claims.claim: EPAC2 regulates synaptic release at PF synapses and is required for presynaptic PF-PC LTP.
claims.source: Moreover, Martín et al., 2020 showed that EPAC2 regulates synaptic release at PF synapses and is required for presynaptic PF-PC LTP.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Martín et al., 2020.

claims.claim: External application of forskolin produced a long-lasting elevation in PF-EPSC amplitude in Atoh1Cre control mice.
claims.source: In Atoh1Cre control mice, external application of forskolin produced a long-lasting elevation in PF-EPSC amplitude (Figure 4A and B), with a peak potentiation of 366 ± 25% (at 48–50 min; n=15; Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A, B, and C.

claims.claim: Simultaneous ablation of EPAC1 and EPAC2 at presynaptic sites prominently affected the synaptic potentiation induced by forskolin application.
claims.source: In contrast, simultaneous ablation of EPAC1 and EPAC2 at presynaptic sites prominently affected the synaptic potentiation induced by forskolin application (162 ± 18% at 48–50 min; n=12; Figure 4A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A, B, and C.

claims.claim: Combined blockade of EPAC and PKA completely eliminated the action of forskolin on EPSC potentiation in Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO PCs.
claims.source: Next, we incubated Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO PCs along with PKA antagonist KT5720 (3 μM) and again examined forskolin-induced EPSC potentiation. In this case, we found that combined blockade of EPAC and PKA completely eliminated the action of forskolin on EPSC potentiation (106 ± 4% at 48–50 min; n=12; Figure 4A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A, B, and C.

claims.claim: The forskolin-induced potentiation in Prkce-cKO PCs was significantly attenuated.
claims.source: Similar to Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO mice, the forskolin-induced potentiation in Prkce-cKO PCs was significantly attenuated (198 ± 5% at 48–50 min; n=12; Figure 4A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A, B, and C.

claims.claim: The remaining potentiation in Prkce-cKO PCs was further blocked by the addition of KT5720.
claims.source: Again, the remaining potentiation was further blocked by the addition of KT5720 (101 ± 3% at 48–50 min; n=12; Figure 4A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A, B, and C.

claims.claim: KT5720 inhibited forskolin-induced potentiation by 15% in Atoh1Cre PCs.
claims.source: The inhibitory effect of KT5720 on forskolin-induced potentiation was also examined by applying it alone in Atoh1Cre PCs. We found that KT5720 inhibited the potentiation by 15%, a smaller effect than that of EPAC or PKCε ablation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: EPAC, PKCε and PKA all mediate cAMP-induced potentiation of transmitter release.
claims.source: Thus, these results indicate that EPAC, PKCε and PKA all mediate cAMP-induced potentiation of transmitter release.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing forskolin-induced potentiation is reduced by EPAC or PKCε deletion and further reduced by PKA inhibition.

claims.claim: Forskolin application led to a significant reduction in PPF ratio of PF-EPSCs in Atoh1Cre mice.
claims.source: Forskolin application led to a significant reduction in PPF ratio of PF-EPSCs in Atoh1Cre mice (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The reduction in PPF ratio by forskolin was significantly less when presynaptic EPAC and PKCε were ablated and KT5720 was added.
claims.source: However, this reduction was significantly less when presynaptic of both types of EPAC as well as PKCε were ablated and KT5720 was added (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: EPAC and PKCε function synergically on the synaptic release at PF-PC synapses.
claims.source: These results highlight that EPAC and PKCε function synergically on the synaptic release at PF-PC synapses.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing combined effects of EPAC and PKCε on forskolin-induced potentiation and PPF changes.

claims.claim: The administration of 8-pCPT was sufficient to potentiate PF-EPSCs by 179 ± 18% in WT PCs.
claims.source: In line with previous work (Kaneko and Takahashi, 2004; Gekel and Neher, 2008), the administration of 8-pCPT was sufficient to potentiate PF-EPSCs by 179 ± 18% and reduce their PPF ratio by 17 ± 3% in WT PCs (n=6; at 18–20 min) (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4D, and is consistent with previous work (Kaneko and Takahashi, 2004; Gekel and Neher, 2008).

claims.claim: The administration of 8-pCPT reduced PPF ratio by 17 ± 3% in WT PCs.
claims.source: In line with previous work (Kaneko and Takahashi, 2004; Gekel and Neher, 2008), the administration of 8-pCPT was sufficient to potentiate PF-EPSCs by 179 ± 18% and reduce their PPF ratio by 17 ± 3% in WT PCs (n=6; at 18–20 min) (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4D, and is consistent with previous work (Kaneko and Takahashi, 2004; Gekel and Neher, 2008).

claims.claim: 8-pCPT-induced potentiation of PF-EPSCs was diminished in Prkce-cKO mice.
claims.source: First, 8-pCPT-induced potentiation of PF-EPSCs was diminished in Prkce-cKO mice, as shown by unchanged PF-EPSCs and PPF (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Co-application of εV1-2 effectively prevented the 8-pCPT-induced synaptic potentiation and change in PPF.
claims.source: Second, co-application of εV1-2 effectively prevented the 8-pCPT-induced synaptic potentiation and change in PPF (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: EPAC-PKCε module and PKA are both downstream effectors of cAMP.
claims.source: In summary, we conclude that EPAC-PKCε module and PKA are both downstream effectors of cAMP, but the EPAC-PKCε module plays the most prominent role in cAMP-triggered EPSC potentiation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing both EPAC-PKCε and PKA contribute to cAMP-induced potentiation.

claims.claim: The EPAC-PKCε module plays the most prominent role in cAMP-triggered EPSC potentiation.
claims.source: In summary, we conclude that EPAC-PKCε module and PKA are both downstream effectors of cAMP, but the EPAC-PKCε module plays the most prominent role in cAMP-triggered EPSC potentiation.

results.result: EPAC1 and EPAC2 are localized to parallel fiber (PF) terminals in cerebellar synaptosomes, as demonstrated by their colocalization with vGluT1, which is enriched at PF terminals. PF synapses constitute the majority (88.8%) of cerebellar synaptosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are supported by immunostaining data (Figure 1B) showing EPAC1/EPAC2 overlap with vGluT1, and quantitative data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing PF synapses constitute 88.8% of synaptosomes. The localization is further validated by citation to prior work establishing vGluT1 as a PF marker.

results.result: EPAC1 and EPAC2 interact with RIM1 and specifically induce threonine phosphorylation of RIM1α without affecting serine phosphorylation. Treatment with 8-pCPT (EPAC activator) increases RIM1 p-Thr but not p-Ser in synaptosomes and HEK cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C11 are supported by co-IP data (Figure 1C) showing EPAC-RIM1 interaction, and western blot data (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) demonstrating selective threonine phosphorylation. The specificity for threonine over serine phosphorylation is consistently shown across multiple experimental systems.

results.result: cAMP induces EPAC-dependent threonine phosphorylation of RIM1. Forskolin increases RIM1 p-Thr, which is blocked by EPAC inhibitor ESI-09. Genetic deletion of EPAC (Rapgef3/4-dKO) significantly reduces RIM1 p-Thr without affecting p-Ser or total RIM1 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C21 are supported by pharmacological experiments (Figure 1E) showing forskolin-induced RIM1 p-Thr is blocked by ESI-09, and genetic experiments (Figure 1F) showing reduced RIM1 p-Thr in EPAC knockout mice. The data consistently demonstrate EPAC is necessary and sufficient for RIM1 threonine phosphorylation.

results.result: EPAC deficiency does not affect cerebellar structure, as lobule thickness and Purkinje cell spine density are unchanged in Rapgef3/4-dKO mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20 are supported by Nissl and Golgi staining data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B) showing no differences in lobule thickness or spine density between WT and EPAC knockout mice. This establishes that the molecular changes occur without gross structural alterations.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that EPAC acts on RIM1 through the Rap1-PLCε-PKCε signaling module, based on prior studies showing this pathway is activated by EPAC in other cell types.
results.evaluation: Claim C23 is explicitly stated as a hypothesis. While claims C24-C26 cite prior work showing EPAC activates this pathway in other cell types, these citations do not directly demonstrate this mechanism operates at cerebellar synapses. The hypothesis requires experimental validation in the current system.

results.result: EPAC activates PKCε specifically at parallel fiber synapses. EPAC expression increases PKCε-S729 phosphorylation but not PKCα phosphorylation in HEK cells. PKCε colocalizes with vGluT1 in synaptosomes, and 8-pCPT treatment increases PKCε-S729 phosphorylation. EPAC deletion reduces PKCε-S729 phosphorylation without affecting PKCα.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C35 are supported by western blot data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, Figure 1I-J) showing EPAC selectively regulates PKCε but not PKCα phosphorylation, and immunostaining data (Figure 1H) showing PKCε localization at PF synapses. The specificity for PKCε over PKCα is consistently demonstrated.

results.result: PKCε binds to RIM1α and regulates its threonine phosphorylation. PKCε expression increases RIM1α p-Thr in HEK cells, and PKCε deletion (Prkce-cKO) reduces RIM1 p-Thr in synaptosomes without affecting p-Ser or total RIM1 levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C41 are supported by co-IP data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B) showing PKCε-RIM1α interaction, and western blot data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C, Figure 1K) demonstrating PKCε regulates RIM1 threonine phosphorylation. The data establish PKCε as a regulator of RIM1 phosphorylation.

results.result: EPAC-induced RIM1 threonine phosphorylation requires PKCε. The PKCε inhibitor εV1-2 blocks 8-pCPT-induced RIM1 p-Thr, while PKCα/β inhibitor Gö6976 has no effect. In Prkce-cKO synaptosomes, 8-pCPT fails to increase RIM1 phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C50 are supported by pharmacological experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D-E) showing selective blockade by PKCε inhibitor but not PKCα/β inhibitor, and genetic experiments (Figure 1L) showing 8-pCPT has no effect in PKCε knockout synaptosomes. The data establish PKCε as the required kinase downstream of EPAC.

results.result: EPAC and PKCε regulate docking of presynaptic vesicles at PF-PC synapses. Deletion of EPAC or PKCε significantly reduces the number of docked vesicles without affecting postsynaptic density, synaptic cleft size, or total vesicle number in terminals.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C61 are supported by electron microscopy data (Figure 2A-B) showing reduced docked vesicles in EPAC and PKCε knockout mice, with specific quantification demonstrating the effect is limited to the docked pool. The structural specificity strengthens the conclusion that EPAC-PKCε regulates vesicle docking.

results.result: EPAC and PKCε are important for presynaptic transmitter release at PF-PC synapses. Deletion of EPAC or PKCε reduces mEPSC frequency without affecting amplitude, decreases release probability (Pr), and reduces evoked EPSCs across all stimulation intensities.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C70 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 2C-F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showing consistent presynaptic deficits in EPAC and PKCε knockout mice. The selective reduction in frequency without amplitude changes, combined with reduced Pr, provides strong evidence for a presynaptic release deficit.

results.result: Deficiency of EPAC or PKCε impairs protein interactions in the Rab3A-RIM1α-Munc13-1 tripartite complex. Both Munc13-1 and Rab3A show significantly weaker binding to RIM1α in EPAC and PKCε knockout synaptosomes, without changes in total protein expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 are supported by co-IP data (Figure 2G-H) showing reduced binding of Munc13-1 and Rab3A to RIM1α in knockout mice, with western blots confirming unchanged total protein levels. The data demonstrate that EPAC-PKCε regulates complex assembly rather than protein expression.

results.result: EPAC and PKCε are sufficient to promote formation of the Rab3A-RIM1α-Munc13-1 tripartite complex. Treatment with 8-pCPT or PKCε activator FR236924 increases binding of Munc13-1 and Rab3A to RIM1, effects that are blocked by PKCε inhibition or deletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C82 are supported by co-IP data (Figure 2I-K) showing pharmacological activation of EPAC or PKCε increases complex formation, with appropriate controls demonstrating PKCε dependence. The bidirectional manipulation (loss and gain of function) strongly supports the conclusion.

results.result: Presynaptic EPAC is required for presynaptic LTP at PF-PC synapses. Tetanus stimulation (8 Hz, 5 min) induces LTP with decreased PPF in control mice, but fails to induce LTP in mice with global or granule cell-specific EPAC deletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C91 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 3B-G) showing LTP induction in controls but not EPAC knockout mice. The use of both global and cell-specific knockouts, combined with PPF measurements indicating presynaptic mechanisms, provides strong evidence for presynaptic EPAC requirement.

results.result: Presynaptic PKCε is required for presynaptic LTP at PF-PC synapses. Genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of PKCε completely blocks the induction of presynaptic LTP.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C95 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 3H-K, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F) showing LTP blockade in PKCε knockout mice and with εV1-2 inhibitor. The convergence of genetic and pharmacological approaches strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: The requirement for EPAC and PKCε in presynaptic LTP is independent of experimental conditions. Presynaptic LTP is blocked in EPAC and PKCε knockout mice across different ages (P21 and 2 months), temperatures (room temperature and 32°C), and calcium concentrations (2 mM and 0.5 mM).
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C109 are supported by extensive electrophysiology data (Figure 3—figure supplements 2-4) showing consistent LTP blockade across multiple experimental conditions. The robustness across conditions strengthens the conclusion that EPAC-PKCε is a core requirement for presynaptic LTP.

results.result: Presynaptic LTP at PF-PC synapses occurs upon a rise in cellular cAMP levels. Preincubation with forskolin (which increases cAMP) prevents further LTP induction by tetanus stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B) showing forskolin pretreatment occludes LTP. This occlusion experiment provides evidence that cAMP elevation is involved in LTP induction, though the interpretation assumes forskolin saturates the relevant pathway.

results.result: EPAC, PKCε, and PKA all mediate cAMP-induced potentiation of transmitter release, with EPAC-PKCε playing the most prominent role. Forskolin induces large EPSC potentiation in controls, which is reduced by EPAC or PKCε deletion and further reduced by PKA inhibition. Combined blockade of EPAC and PKA completely eliminates forskolin's effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C120 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 4A-C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing graded reductions in forskolin-induced potentiation with EPAC/PKCε deletion and PKA inhibition. The quantitative comparison demonstrates EPAC-PKCε has a larger effect than PKA, supporting the conclusion about relative contributions.

results.result: EPAC and PKCε function synergistically on synaptic release at PF-PC synapses. Forskolin reduces PPF ratio in controls, but this reduction is significantly attenuated when EPAC, PKCε, and PKA are all blocked.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C123 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 4C) showing PPF changes parallel the EPSC amplitude changes. The PPF data provide additional evidence for presynaptic mechanisms and support the synergistic function interpretation.

results.result: Direct EPAC activation with 8-pCPT is sufficient to potentiate PF-EPSCs and reduce PPF, effects that require PKCε. The 8-pCPT-induced potentiation is abolished in PKCε knockout mice or by PKCε inhibitor εV1-2.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C129 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 4D-F) showing 8-pCPT effects are blocked by PKCε deletion or inhibition. The data establish EPAC-PKCε as the dominant pathway for cAMP-induced potentiation, with PKA playing a secondary role.

results.result: Presynaptic EPAC and PKCε are not required for postsynaptic LTP at PF-PC synapses. A 1 Hz stimulation protocol induces LTP without PPF changes in both control and mice with presynaptic deletion of EPAC or PKCε.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C145 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 5B-J) showing postsynaptic LTP is intact in mice with presynaptic EPAC or PKCε deletion. The unchanged PPF confirms the postsynaptic nature of this LTP form, and the intact LTP demonstrates specificity of EPAC-PKCε for presynaptic mechanisms.

results.result: Presynaptic EPAC and PKCε are not required for postsynaptic LTD at PF-PC synapses. The standard LTD induction protocol successfully induces LTD without PPF changes in both control and mice with presynaptic deletion of EPAC or PKCε.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C144 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 6B-J) showing postsynaptic LTD is intact in mice with presynaptic EPAC or PKCε deletion. The unchanged PPF confirms the postsynaptic nature of this LTD form, further demonstrating the specificity of EPAC-PKCε for presynaptic plasticity.

results.result: Presynaptic deletion of EPAC or PKCε impairs basic motor performance when visual and vestibular systems are tested separately (OKR and VOR), but not when engaged simultaneously (VVOR). Both Rapgef3/4-dKO and Prkce-cKO mice show deficits in OKR and VOR gain and phase, but normal VVOR.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C158 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 7B-G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C) showing consistent deficits in OKR and VOR but not VVOR across multiple mouse lines. The selective impairment pattern suggests EPAC-PKCε is important when sensory systems operate independently but can be compensated when they work together.

results.result: EPAC and PKCε are required for VOR phase reversal learning. Control mice show proper gain decrease and phase reversal during training, while Rapgef3/4-dKO, Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO, and Prkce-cKO mice show smaller gain reductions and prominent deficits in phase reversal learning, particularly on days 2-5.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C165 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 7I-J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) showing impaired VOR adaptation in EPAC and PKCε knockout mice. The temporal pattern (intact day 1, impaired days 2-5) suggests EPAC-PKCε is particularly important for consolidation or expression of learned motor adaptations.

results.result: The EPAC-PKCε signaling cascade regulates presynaptic LTP and motor learning through a novel mechanism involving threonine phosphorylation of RIM1α and assembly of the Rab3A-RIM1α-Munc13-1 complex. This pathway is critical for presynaptic LTP at PF-PC synapses and for cerebellar motor behavior, enriching the spectrum of cerebellar learning mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C173 represent the main conclusions of the study, which are supported by the convergence of molecular (phosphorylation, protein interactions), structural (vesicle docking), electrophysiological (LTP, release), and behavioral (motor learning) data. The comprehensive multi-level evidence strongly supports the proposed signaling cascade and its functional importance.
